newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China backup for HK stocks seen having small impact.
newsitem.headline: China backup for HK stocks seen having small impact.

text.p: Mainland Chinese money has been flowing into Hong Kong and will continue to support local stock prices, analysts said on Wednesday, but a contingency fund to ward off stock market volatility would have limited impact.

The Beijing-backed Ta Kung Po newspaper reported on Tuesday that China has set up a contingency fund to bail out Hong Kong's stock market if it experiences a sharp drop after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997.

"There was always the belief that the Chinese government would stand behind the Hong Kong market because it remains the case that the Hong Kong market is the key barometer of public sentiment," said David Semple, equity strategist at Peregrine Research Institute.
A support fund "can in some circumstances calm down the market, but it does not alter the ultimate supply and demand position unless the support fund has a long time frame", he said.
Analysts said stock prices in the territory are already being buoyed by the participation of Chinese enterprises in the market and the local economy, particularly the property market.
The blue chip Hang Seng index hit record high levels this month, driven by corporate earnings and rising liquidity.
"Market performance is pretty much determined by underlying fundamentals," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.
If Hong Kong stocks did sell off next year, a contingency fund could only provide short-term relief, analysts said.
"I don't think China has the ability to affect the Hong Kong market if anything but for very, very short periods of time," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.
"The market is by Chinese standards very big. There is no way that China has the financial wherewithal to drive the market long term like that," he added.
The capitalisation of the Hong Kong stock market is about HK$3.05 trillion (US$395 billion), according to the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong.
"It's a big market. It would take a lot of money to support it," said Janice Wallace, co-head of research at Goldman Sachs.
During the last big market downturns, in 1987 and during the 1989 crackdown on student-led protests in Beijing, Chinese institutions came in to support the market, she said.
"I think historically, China has always been involved in the market when it has sold off, and there is no reason to expect that would not happen in the future," she said.

Wallace said support was likely to be seen in the form of continued participation from China enterprises. "We expect China enterprises to become far more active here anyway, and they are obviously going to take advantage of market weakness."
Mays said aggressive intervention would probably hurt the Hong Kong market more than anything else.
"If the government is seen to interfere it could distract foreign investors from Hong Kong, (which) is the most sensitive market in Asia to foreign investment," he said.
"Reduced volatility is not necessarily good," he added. "If anything, high volatilty presents good return opportunity."

Mays said the comment on the contingency fund, reportedly made by Zheng Wantong, a Chinese Communist Party official, was "inappropriate". "It is probably a trial balloon and it should not have been floated and it should be ignored," he said.
